propositions.text: Whether police conduct in this case was an abuse of statutory stop and search powers under the Saskatchewan Highways and Transportation Act.
propositions.quote: This appeal is concerned with police search powers incident to random stops under the Saskatchewan Highways and Transportation Act, 1997, S.S. 1997, c. H-3.01 (“H&TA”), and, in particular, whether the police conduct in this case amounted to an abuse of their statutory stop and search powers

propositions.text: Whether evidence of drug dealing and proceeds of crime should be excluded under sections 8 or 9 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
propositions.quote: so as to render evidence of drug dealing and the “proceeds of crime” inadmissible under s. 8 or s. 9 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the appeal concerns whether police abused statutory stop and search powers and if evidence should be excluded under Charter sections 8 or 9.

propositions.text: Appellants were stopped on the Trans-Canada Highway; truck registration and fuel sticker issues were found.
propositions.quote: The appellants were travelling eastward along the Saskatchewan portion of the Trans-Canada Highway with a passenger (now deceased) in an empty 53-foot commercial tractor-trailer unit licensed in Quebec...the truck’s registration was not prorated to include the province. The appropriate fuel sticker had expired.

propositions.text: Nolet produced an incomplete logbook indicating operation east of Manitoba border.
propositions.quote: The appellant Nolet produced a logbook that was incomplete but indicated that the truck normally operated east of the Manitoba border.

propositions.text: Police found $115,000 cash and 392 pounds of marijuana in a secret compartment in the trailer.
propositions.quote: in the end the police found $115,000 in cash in the truck and 392 pounds of marijuana, valued at somewhere between $1.1 million to $1.5 million, concealed in a secret compartment in the trailer.

propositions.text: Appellants charged with trafficking, possession for trafficking, and possession of proceeds of crime.
propositions.quote: The appellants were charged in a multi-count indictment alleging (1) trafficking, (2) possession of marijuana for the purposes of trafficking, and (3) possession of proceeds of crime in excess of $5,000.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Charter breaches and excluded evidence, acquitting appellants.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found Charter breaches and excluded the evidence (2006 SKQB 393, 283 Sask. R. 159 ). She acquitted the appellants.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal reversed trial judge, with one dissenting judge.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal, Jackson J.A. dissenting in part, reversed (2009 SKCA 8, 320 Sask. R. 179 ).

paragraphs.summary: The Court summarizes facts: appellants stopped, irregularities found, large cash and marijuana discovered; trial judge excluded evidence, Court of Appeal reversed.

propositions.text: Random vehicle checks must be limited to their intended purpose and not become unreasonable searches.
propositions.quote: Clearly random checks of vehicles for highway purposes must be limited to their intended purpose and cannot be turned into “an unfounded general inquisition or an unreasonable search”: R. v. Mellenthin, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 615, at p. 624.

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites precedent that random vehicle checks must be limited and not become unreasonable searches.

propositions.text: Court must analyze police-appellant interactions step by step to determine if police stayed within authority.
propositions.quote: It is necessary for a court to proceed step by step through the interactions of the police and the appellants from the initial stop onwards to determine whether...the police stayed within their authority

propositions.text: The majority reached the correct conclusion and the appeal should be dismissed.
propositions.quote: Analysed in this way, I believe the majority reached the correct conclusion. I would dismiss the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the need for stepwise analysis and finds the majority decision correct, dismissing the appeal.

propositions.text: On Feb 16, 2004, appellants stopped in random check; driver Vatsis, Nolet passenger, Blain in sleeping compartment.
propositions.quote: On February 16, 2004, a little after 11:00 p.m., the appellants and passenger Marc Blain were stopped by an RCMP officer engaged in a random check under the H&TA. The appellant Vatsis was driving...Nolet was in the passenger seat. Blain...was behind the front seats in a sleeping compartment.

propositions.text: Officer noticed expired fuel sticker, requested licence, logbook, registration; Nolet listed as co-driver, Blain not mentioned.
propositions.quote: The officer noticed the expired IFTA fuel sticker...He requested the driver’s licence, logbook...and vehicle registration. The documents produced by Vatsis listed Nolet as a co-driver. Blain was not mentioned

propositions.text: Nolet said truck was empty, having unloaded cargo; logbook did not record these stops and did not match bills of lading; odometer numbers seemed fiddled.
propositions.quote: Nolet told the officer they were now travelling empty having unloaded cargo in Edmonton and Moose Jaw...These stops were not recorded in the logbook...There seemed to the officer to have been some fiddling with the odometer numbers.

paragraphs.summary: The Court recounts the initial stop details: expired sticker, document requests, discrepancies in logbook and odometer.

propositions.text: Failure to prorate vehicle registration is a provincial infraction; Nolet said vehicle usually operated east of Ontario.
propositions.quote: The failure to prorate the vehicle registration for commercial driving in Saskatchewan is also a provincial infraction...Nolet said that the vehicle did not usually go any further west than Ontario.

propositions.text: A commercial vehicle without proper permits can be prohibited from further travel in the province under s. 66(1) of the H&TA.
propositions.quote: A commercial vehicle without the requisite permits can immediately be prohibited from further travel within the province (s. 66(1) of the H&TA).

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes registration infraction and legal authority to prohibit vehicle travel without permits.

propositions.text: Officer asked to inspect trailer; Nolet agreed; trailer was empty but looked odd to officer.
propositions.quote: The officer asked whether he could inspect the trailer. Nolet agreed. The trailer was empty. The police officer thought it “looked odd” but “at that point I couldn’t put my finger on it . . . it didn’t appear right”

paragraphs.summary: The Court states the officer inspected the trailer with consent and found it empty but suspicious.

propositions.text: Officer alone decided not to enter trailer but to inspect tractor documents to confirm logbooks and bills of lading.
propositions.quote: The officer, being alone, decided not to enter the trailer but to pursue the issue of defective trucking documents...I had hoped to obtain documents to confirm or dispute the contents of the log books, . . . previous bills of ladin[g], tickets, those types of documents.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes the officer's decision to inspect tractor documents to verify logbooks and bills of lading.

propositions.text: Officer did not seek consent for search of tractor interior, assuming cooperation continued.
propositions.quote: The officer did not seek consent from the appellants for this search — he testified it was because the occupants had cooperated so far.

propositions.text: Officer found a duffle bag in sleeping compartment, opened it expecting documents but found $115,000 cash.
propositions.quote: Immediately behind the driver’s seat in the sleeping compartment, he found a small Roots blue and white duffle bag...However the duffle bag contained money — $115,000 — bundled in small denominations

propositions.text: Officer testified cash packaging typical of drug transactions and arrested appellants for possession of proceeds of crime.
propositions.quote: The officer testified that in his experience this sort of packaging of cash was typical of drug transactions and he immediately placed the appellants and Blain under arrest for possession of the proceeds of crime.

propositions.text: Nine minutes elapsed since initial stop when arrest occurred.
propositions.quote: Nine minutes had elapsed since the initial stop.

paragraphs.summary: The Court recounts the officer's warrantless search of a duffle bag, discovery of cash, and arrest within nine minutes.

propositions.text: Backup summoned; trailer inspected again; hidden compartment discovered due to interior length discrepancy.
propositions.quote: Police back-up was summoned. The trailer was inspected again. At this point the officers discovered that the interior measurement of the trailer was about three feet shorter than the exterior length, indicating the presence of a hidden compartment.

propositions.text: Appellants directed to drive to nearest RCMP detachment, arriving just before midnight.
propositions.quote: The officers directed the appellants to drive the rig about 10 kilometres to the nearest RCMP detachment, where they arrived just before midnight.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states backup was called, hidden compartment found, and appellants taken to RCMP detachment.

propositions.text: About 1.5 hours later, officers opened hidden compartment and found 392 pounds of marijuana valued at $1.1 to $1.5 million.
propositions.quote: About an hour and a half later, the officers opened up the hidden compartment. It contained 392 pounds of packaged cannabis marijuana valued at between $1.1 and $1.5 million

paragraphs.summary: The Court reports discovery of large quantity of marijuana in hidden compartment at RCMP detachment.

propositions.text: Next day, RCMP Corporal Houston inventoried tractor-trailer contents, finding additional documentation and paraphernalia.
propositions.quote: The following day around 1:00 p.m., RCMP Corporal Caroline Houston...made an inventory...She discovered considerable additional documentation relevant to the H&TA offences, including factory decals, registration papers and permits for different companies

propositions.text: Paraphernalia could make truck look like a completely different truck.
propositions.quote: This paraphernalia when applied to the exterior would make the truck look like “a completely different truck”

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes inventory found additional documents and paraphernalia that could disguise the truck's identity.

propositions.text: Police never obtained a search warrant during inspections, searches, and seizures.
propositions.quote: At no time during this series of inspections, searches and seizures did the police obtain a search warrant.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states police did not obtain any search warrant during the entire process.

propositions.text: Section 8 of Charter protects against unreasonable search or seizure; section 9 protects against arbitrary detention.
propositions.quote: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms 8. Everyone has the right to be secure against unreasonable search or seizure. 9. Everyone has the right not to be arbitrarily detained or imprisoned.

propositions.text: H&TA sections 63(5) and (6) authorize peace officers to stop, search, and seize vehicles with reasonable grounds of contravention.
propositions.quote: 63 . . . (5) Where the peace officer...has reasonable grounds to believe that a vehicle is being operated in contravention...may: (a) request or signal to stop; (b) search the vehicle; (c) seize anything that may be evidence... (6) The person...shall: (a) stop; (b) permit search; (c) provide information

propositions.text: Section 64(1) allows a justice to issue a warrant for search and seizure if reasonable grounds exist.
propositions.quote: 64(1) Where a justice of the peace...is satisfied...that there are reasonable grounds...may issue a warrant to...enter and search...seize anything that may be evidence

propositions.text: Section 64(2) authorizes search and seizure with a warrant, including opening receptacles and examining records.
propositions.quote: (2) With a warrant...may: (a) enter and search... (b) search any vehicle... (c) open and examine any trunk, box, bag... (d) require production of records... (e) remove, for the purpose of making copie

paragraphs.summary: The Court sets out relevant Charter rights and H&TA statutory provisions on stop, search, seizure, and warrants.

propositions.text: Trial judge held police inspection powers did not permit warrantless search of duffle bag without reasonable or probable grounds of criminal offence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge held that the police inspection powers...did not extend to permit a warrantless search of the small duffle bag...where the officer had no reasonable or probable grounds to believe that criminal offences had been committed.

propositions.text: Expectation of privacy in commercial vehicles is less than private vehicles but still entitled to Charter protection.
propositions.quote: While the expectation of privacy in a commercial vehicle is generally less than in a private vehicle...even this lesser privacy interest was entitled to Charter protection.

propositions.text: Officer's concerns about trailer alterations related to suspected criminal activity, not primarily regulatory matters.
propositions.quote: Such a concern does not relate primarily to commercial trucking regulations. It relates to suspected criminal activity.

propositions.text: Officer was more interested in criminal activity than regulatory infractions when continuing investigation.
propositions.quote: it does appear that the officer was more interested in looking for evidence of criminal activity than for contraventions of commercial trucking regulations.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found warrantless search of duffle bag unreasonable, with officer focused on criminal activity, not regulatory concerns.

propositions.text: Trial judge found warrantless searches unreasonable and excluded evidence; appellants acquitted.
propositions.quote: In the trial judge’s view, the warrantless searches were unreasonable and the evidence of the money and the marijuana was excluded. The appellants were acquitted.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge excluded evidence from warrantless searches and acquitted the appellants.

propositions.text: Majority of Court of Appeal held mere hunch about trailer alteration did not taint lawful regulatory search.
propositions.quote: In the majority view, a mere hunch or speculation that a trailer had been altered or refabricated...did not taint an otherwise lawful regulatory search.

propositions.text: Appellants failed to prove police exploited regulatory inspection as pretext for criminal search.
propositions.quote: The appellants had not established that the police were exploiting the highway regulatory inspection as a convenient pretext

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal majority found no pretextual abuse of regulatory search powers by police.

propositions.text: Detention was not arbitrary; search for documents authorized by law; no s. 8 Charter violation.
propositions.quote: The detention was not arbitrary. The search for documents was authorized by law. The police had not violated the appellants’ reasonable expectation of privacy. There was no infringement of s. 8 .

propositions.text: Money found in duffle bag should not have been excluded; marijuana found incident to lawful arrest was admissible.
propositions.quote: The money found in the duffle bag should not have been excluded from evidence. The marijuana was located in a search incidental to a lawful arrest.

propositions.text: Search incident to lawful arrest is an exception to warrantless search presumption of unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: This is an exception to the principle that warrantless searches are prima facie unreasonable.

propositions.text: Both marijuana and cash evidence should have been admitted; new trial ordered.
propositions.quote: In the majority view, the two items of evidence...ought both to have been admitted into evidence. A new trial was ordered.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal majority found no Charter breach, admitted evidence, and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: Jackson J.A. held police could not rely on regulatory search power once focus shifted to criminal activity.
propositions.quote: Jackson J.A. concluded that the trial judge did not err in holding that the police officer could not rely on a regulatory search power once his “focus” became criminal activity.

propositions.text: Police cannot search for contraband under regulatory search authority.
propositions.quote: A police officer could not search for contraband with that as the purpose or one of the defined purposes of the search, because the search authority extended to regulatory matters only.

propositions.text: Jackson J.A. agreed searches incident to lawful arrest would be lawful.
propositions.quote: Jackson J.A. agreed with the majority that if the arrest had been lawful, the searches undertaken as incident to that arrest would have been lawful as well.

paragraphs.summary: Jackson J.A. dissented in part, holding regulatory search power cannot be used for criminal searches but incident-to-arrest searches lawful.

propositions.text: Jackson J.A. distinguished between money and marijuana for exclusion under s. 24(2) Charter.
propositions.quote: Applying s. 24(2) of the Charter , Jackson J.A. drew a distinction between the money and the marijuana.

propositions.text: Cash rightly excluded; marijuana admitted; acquittal on proceeds of crime charge sustained; new trial on drug charges ordered.
propositions.quote: In her view, the cash was rightly excluded, but the marijuana ought to have been admitted. Thus...she would have sustained the acquittal on the “proceeds of crime” charge, but set aside the acquittals...and ordered a new trial in relation to the drug charges only.

paragraphs.summary: Jackson J.A. would exclude cash but admit marijuana, sustaining acquittal on proceeds charge and ordering new trial on drug charges.

propositions.text: Whether warrantless searches during random roadside stops are reasonable under s. 8 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: A warrantless search is presumptively unreasonable and contrary to s. 8 of the Charter , which guarantees to everyone “the right to be secure against unreasonable search or seizure”.

propositions.text: Crown must prove on balance of probabilities that warrantless search is authorized by law, law is reasonable, and manner of search is reasonable.
propositions.quote: the Crown must establish on a balance of probabilities that the search was authorized by law, that the law itself is reasonable, and that the manner in which the search was carried out was reasonable

paragraphs.summary: The Court states warrantless searches during random stops are presumptively unreasonable under s. 8, requiring Crown to prove legality and reasonableness.

propositions.text: Whether random vehicle stops violate s. 9 of the Charter against arbitrary detention.
propositions.quote: A random vehicle stop on the highway is, by definition, an arbitrary detention

propositions.text: Random stops are arbitrary detentions per prior cases Dedman, Hufsky, Ladouceur (Ont.), Mellenthin, Harris.
propositions.quote: Dedman v. The Queen, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 2; R. v. Hufsky, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 621; R. v. Ladouceur, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 1257 (hereinafter “Ladouceur (Ont.)”); Mellenthin; and R. v. Harris, 2007 ONCA 574, 87 O.R. (3d) 214.

propositions.text: Detention justified under s. 1 only if police act within limited highway-related purposes.
propositions.quote: The detention will only be justified under s. 1 of the Charter (Hufsky, at p. 637) if the police act within the limited highway-related purposes for which the powers were conferred (Ladouceur (Ont.), per Cory J., at p. 1287).

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains random stops are arbitrary detentions under s. 9 but may be justified under s. 1 if limited to highway-related purposes.

propositions.text: Random roadside stops must be limited to their intended purposes; they do not authorize general searches.
propositions.quote: Random roadside stops must be limited to their intended purposes. “A check stop does not and cannot constitute a general search warrant for searching every vehicle, driver and passenger that is pulled over”

propositions.text: Whether police authority at each step from stop to discovery of evidence was lawful and reasonable under s. 8 and s. 9 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: it thus becomes necessary to examine the authority claimed by the police at each step ... to determine at what point, if at all, the police infringed the rights of the appellants under s. 8 or s. 9 of the Charter

propositions.text: A roadside stop is dynamic; new information may justify further police action or end the stop.
propositions.quote: A roadside stop is not a static event. Information as it emerges may entitle the police to proceed further, or ... end their enquiries and allow the vehicle to resume its journey.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states random stops must be limited to intended purposes and police authority at each step must be examined for Charter compliance.

propositions.text: Whether the search of the duffle bag was authorized by s. 63(5) of the H&TA is important but insufficient alone.
propositions.quote: Much of the debate on the appeal focussed on whether the search of the duffle bag was or was not covered by s. 63(5) of the H&TA. This inquiry is important but not sufficient.

propositions.text: Distinction between existence of police power and whether its exercise violates s. 8 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: A distinction must be drawn between the existence of a police power and the further issue of whether that power ... is exercised in violation of s. 8 of the Charter

propositions.text: Focusing only on H&TA powers may neglect Charter concerns; focusing only on Charter may neglect whether police had power to search.
propositions.quote: An exclusive focus on police powers under the H&TA may not give adequate weight to Charter concerns. Equally, restricting the Court’s focus to the Charter may distract attention from ... whether the police possessed the power to conduct a search in the first place.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains that both police statutory powers and Charter rights must be considered regarding the duffle bag search.

propositions.text: Police can randomly stop persons for driving-related reasons like checking licence, sobriety, vehicle fitness.
propositions.quote: the police officers can randomly stop persons for “reasons related to driving a car such as checking the driver’s licence and insurance, the sobriety of the driver and the mechanical fitness of the vehicle”

propositions.text: Courts below held appellants’ truck stop was valid for H&TA document check; issue no longer seriously disputed.
propositions.quote: The courts below held that the appellants’ truck was stopped for the valid purpose of carrying out an H&TA document check, and this issue is no longer seriously in dispute.

propositions.text: Stop was valid and case distinguishable from Harrison where accused was pulled over for no valid purpose.
propositions.quote: The stop was valid. On this basis, the case is readily distinguishable from our Court’s recent ruling in R. v. Harrison, 2009 SCC 34, where the accused had been pulled over for no valid purpose.

propositions.text: Police exceeded powers in Ladouceur (Sask.) where random stop aimed at detecting contraband and staffed by multiple agencies.
propositions.quote: The police equally exceed their powers in the Saskatchewan case of R. v. Ladouceur, 2002 SKCA 73 ... The random stop program in Ladouceur (Sask.) was designed as a “comprehensive check for criminal activity” and was therefore fatally flawed from the outset.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes police can stop for driving-related reasons; the appellants’ stop was valid unlike in Ladouceur (Sask.) where powers were exceeded.

propositions.text: Random stop program here was related to legitimate highway purposes and did not violate appellants’ s. 9 rights.
propositions.quote: the random stop program was directly related to legitimate highway purposes ... did not violate the s. 9 rights of the appellants

propositions.text: Citing Ladouceur (Ont.) and Orbanski for principle that highway-related stops can be justified under s. 1.
propositions.quote: Ladouceur (Ont.), at p. 1287; Orbanski, at para. 41.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the stop was related to legitimate highway purposes and did not violate s. 9 rights, citing prior cases.

propositions.text: s. 32(1) Motor Carrier Act authorizes peace officer to order vehicle or cargo examination and tests.
propositions.quote: Section 32(1) of The Motor Carrier Act authorizes a peace officer to “order the driver or owner of a vehicle to submit the vehicle ... or the cargo being carried on such a vehicle to any examination and tests that the peace officer considers necessary”.

propositions.text: s. 63(5) H&TA allows warrantless search if officer has reasonable grounds to believe vehicle is operated in contravention of regulatory requirements.
propositions.quote: s. 63(5) of the H&TA provides that if a police officer “has reasonable grounds to believe that a vehicle is being operated in contravention” of regulatory requirements, he may conduct a warrantless search

propositions.text: Regulatory offences include vehicle markings, driver’s log contents, hours of duty, trip inspection reports.
propositions.quote: “an offence” refers to H&TA provisions that include regulation of the manner in which any part of a vehicle or its load is to be marked or labelled; the contents of a driver’s log and the manner in which a driver’s log is to be kept and maintained; the number of hours a driver can be on duty or drive; and, the classes or types of vehicles for which a trip inspection report is to be completed

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains statutory authority for warrantless searches under Motor Carrier Act and H&TA for regulatory offences.

propositions.text: Officer quickly had reasonable grounds to believe appellants violated H&TA due to licence, fuel sticker, and logbook issues.
propositions.quote: the officer quickly obtained reasonable grounds to believe that the appellants were operating the truck in violation of the H&TA, having regard to the lack of a truck licence valid in Saskatchewan, the display of an expired fuel sticker and inconsistent entries in the driver’s logbook.

propositions.text: At time of cab search, officer was within statutory authority to search for further evidence of H&TA offences.
propositions.quote: At the time the officer began to investigate the cab of the tractor unit, it was quite within his statutory authority to search for further evidence related to H&TA offences.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the officer had reasonable grounds and statutory authority to search the cab for H&TA offences.

propositions.text: Continued detention and search of tractor-trailer rig for relevant papers was authorized and initially reasonable.
propositions.quote: the continued detention of the appellants was not arbitrary and the search of the tractor-trailer rig for relevant papers was authorized by s. 63(5)(b). At least initially, they were not unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the continued detention and search were authorized and initially reasonable.

propositions.text: Drivers have some expectation of privacy in sleeping area of tractor-trailer cab, including behind front seats.
propositions.quote: drivers ordinarily have some expectation of privacy in the sleeping area of a cab of the tractor-trailer, including the space behind the front seats where the duffle bag with the money was found.

propositions.text: Reasonable expectation of privacy assessed by totality of circumstances; onus on Charter claimant to prove it.
propositions.quote: Whether or not an individual has a subjective expectation of privacy, and whether or not that expectation is objectively reasonable, is an assessment to be made having regard to the totality of the circumstances ... The onus of proof of such reasonable expectation, to a probability standard, lies on the Charter claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds drivers have some privacy expectation in sleeping area; reasonableness assessed by totality of circumstances with onus on claimant.

propositions.text: Court may presume individuals expect some privacy in truck sleeping quarters as temporary mobile home.
propositions.quote: the court may presume that individuals would expect a measure of privacy in what, for a long-distance trucker, suffices as a temporary mobile home.

propositions.text: Living quarters should not be Charter-free zone; expectation is objectively reasonable.
propositions.quote: The expectation is objectively reasonable because living quarters, however rudimentary, should not be classified as a Charter -free zone

propositions.text: Expectation of privacy is low because cab is both rest and work place, subject to frequent random checks.
propositions.quote: the level of expectation is necessarily low because the cab of a tractor-trailer rig is not only a place of rest but a place of work, and the whole of the cab is therefore vulnerable to frequent random checks

propositions.text: Wilkinson J.A. noted drivers know of mandatory inspections and searches under transportation legislation.
propositions.quote: Wilkinson J.A. pointed out, “[k]nowledge of the transportation legislation is a requirement to be licensed as a driver. The [appellants] would be well aware of the possibility of mandatory inspections and searches

propositions.text: There can be little expectation of privacy in sleeping area, especially if travelling in violation of regulations.
propositions.quote: there can be little expectation of privacy, even in the sleeping area of a truck (particularly one which is travelling in violation of relevant highway regulations).

propositions.text: Occupants know or ought to know a stop may lead to a search and should govern themselves accordingly.
propositions.quote: A stop may quickly precipitate a search, and the occupants either know or ought to know of that reality and govern themselves accordingly.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds some privacy expectation in truck sleeping area but low due to work nature and regulatory inspections.

propositions.text: Appellants argue lawful investigation became unlawful when officer suspected criminal activity and searched duffle bag.
propositions.quote: The appellants ... say it fell outside any valid regulatory purpose.

propositions.text: Trial judge found officer’s search of duffle bag was predominantly for illegal criminal activity, outside valid regulatory purpose.
propositions.quote: the trial judge found ... that the policeman’s search of the duffle bag should be attributed predominantly to his interest in illegal criminal activity

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue and trial judge found the search of the duffle bag was mainly for criminal investigation, not regulatory purpose.

propositions.text: Officer admitted his job included interest in contraband and only suspected secret compartment after finding money.
propositions.quote: he testified that it was only “at that point” of finding the money that he believed “there was a good possibility there was a secret compartment in the trailer”

paragraphs.summary: The officer testified he was interested in contraband and suspected a secret compartment only after finding money.

propositions.text: Whether officer exceeded s. 63(5) authority when suspicion of criminal activity arose during search.
propositions.quote: The first question is whether the police officer, in continuing the search, exceeded his s. 63(5) authority when he reached the point of suspicion.

propositions.text: Whether the search was unreasonable in relation to Charter privacy interests despite statutory authority.
propositions.quote: The second question is whether what he did ... was unreasonable in relation to the protected Charter privacy interests of the accused in the sleeping area of the cab.

propositions.text: Statutory authority and reasonableness of exercise are distinct issues.
propositions.quote: The statutory authority for the search and the reasonableness of its exercise are two distinct issues.

paragraphs.summary: The Court poses two questions: whether officer exceeded statutory authority and whether the search was reasonable under the Charter.

propositions.text: Trial judge found officer was more interested in criminal activity than regulatory infractions despite some regulatory concerns.
propositions.quote: it does appear that the officer was more interested in looking for evidence of criminal activity than for contraventions of commercial trucking regulations

propositions.text: Trial judge discussed dual purpose searches and whether dominant criminal purpose invalidates regulatory search or vice versa.
propositions.quote: This led to a discussion about “dual purpose” searches, and whether a “dominant” criminal law purpose would invalidate an otherwise valid regulatory search or, on the contrary, a legitimate regulatory purpose could “sanitize” or “cleanse” an unlawful criminal law purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found the officer’s dominant interest was criminal and discussed dual purpose search validity.

propositions.text: Wilkinson J.A. found dual purpose debate unhelpful; lawful aim cannot be a pretext for unlawful aim.
propositions.quote: the lawful aim cannot be used as a pretext, ruse, or subterfuge to perpetuate the unlawful aim.

propositions.text: Wilkinson J.A. held this case not like Ladouceur (Sask.) where checkstops had a facade of lawful aim for unlawful purpose.
propositions.quote: What happened here, in her view, is not within the mischief contemplated by ... Ladouceur (Sask.) that “it is important not to encourage the establishment of checkstops where a nominally lawful aim is but a plausible facade for an unlawful aim”

paragraphs.summary: Wilkinson J.A. rejected dual purpose test, holding lawful aims cannot mask unlawful ones; this case differs from Ladouceur (Sask.).

propositions.text: RCMP officers naturally interested in criminal and provincial infractions; lawful search not converted by expectation of finding drugs.
propositions.quote: the lawful search was not converted into an unlawful or an unreasonable search because the officers, in addition, had the expectation that the search might also uncover drugs

paragraphs.summary: Wilkinson J.A. noted lawful searches are not unlawful simply because officers expect to find drugs.

propositions.text: In Brown, police used H&TA powers to stop bikers suspected of criminal activity; stop upheld but improper additional purpose invalidates stop.
propositions.quote: While I can find no sound reason for invalidating an otherwise proper stop because the police used the opportunity afforded by that stop to further some other legitimate interest, I do see strong policy reasons for invalidating a stop where the police have an additional improper purpose.

paragraphs.summary: Brown case held proper stops are valid despite other legitimate interests, but stops with improper additional purposes should be invalidated.

propositions.text: Police power abused if exercised violating Charter rights; valid regulatory purpose does not excuse Charter violation.
propositions.quote: Police power ... is abused when it is exercised in a manner that violates the Charter rights of an accused ... A valid regulatory purpose ... would not sanitize or excuse a Charter violation.

propositions.text: This framework is better than the trial judge’s predominant purpose test.
propositions.quote: This is a better framework of analysis, in my opinion, than the “predominant purpose” test applied here by the trial judge.

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds police violate Charter if power abused; valid regulatory purpose cannot excuse Charter breach; this is better than predominant purpose test.

propositions.text: In Law, police powers authorized by statute; issue was whether hidden intentions made search unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The distinguishing feature of Annett, however, is that the full scope of the officers’ search was authorized by statute; thus, the only issue was whether their hidden intentions rendered the search unreasonable.

propositions.text: Distinction between police powers and Charter compliance is important.
propositions.quote: Of interest for present purposes, however, is the distinction noted by the Court between police powers and Charter compliance.

paragraphs.summary: The Court cites Law to distinguish police statutory powers from Charter reasonableness of search.

propositions.text: Whether the officer's search of the duffle bag infringed the appellants' reasonable expectations of privacy.
propositions.quote: the issue is whether the officer’s search of the duffle bag infringed the reasonable expectations of privacy of the appellants

propositions.text: The search did not infringe the appellants' reasonable expectations of privacy given the totality of the circumstances.
propositions.quote: I do not think that it did, having regard to the totality of the circumstances as they had progressed to the time of that search

propositions.text: Wilkinson J.A. said the question is not about determining which purpose is predominant or subordinate.
propositions.quote: I agree with Wilkinson J.A. that the question is not “determining which purpose is predominate or subordinate” (para. 85)

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Wilkinson J.A. that the search's legality depends on privacy expectations, which were not infringed here.

propositions.text: The trial judge set the barrier for ongoing police investigation too high, requiring consent or grounds to continue search after suspicion arose.
propositions.quote: the trial judge... set the barrier to the ongoing police investigation too high... he required either informed consent or reasonable and probable grounds to continue searching... neither of which existed

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge required too high a standard for continuing the search after suspicion arose, according to the trial judge's own words.

propositions.text: The officer's interest in contraband did not render the H&TA search unlawful or unreasonable under s. 8 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: I do not agree that the officer’s concurrent interest in contraband... rendered the H&TA search unlawful or unreasonable within the scope of s. 8 of the Charter

propositions.text: Commercial drivers know police can conduct random stops and searches; commercial trucking is highly regulated.
propositions.quote: Commercial drivers are well aware of the police authority to conduct random stops and to search a vehicle for evidence of infractions. Commercial trucking is a highly regulated industry

propositions.text: Breaching a law does not reduce legitimate privacy expectations under s. 8.
propositions.quote: Breaching a law will not in itself reduce an individual’s legitimate privacy expectations

propositions.text: Expectation that a search might uncover drugs does not convert a Charter-compliant regulatory search into a violation.
propositions.quote: the expectation that the search might also uncover drugs” (p. 335) did not convert a Charter -compliant regulatory search into a Charter violation

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the search lawful under s. 8, noting commercial drivers' awareness and that law breaches don't reduce privacy rights.

propositions.text: The officer had reasonable grounds to open the duffle bag after preliminary evaluation of its contents relevant to the regulatory search.
propositions.quote: the officer did not proceed immediately to open the bag without some preliminary evaluation of its likely relevance to the regulatory search

propositions.text: Opening the bag was not unreasonable given the appellants' limited privacy interest; cash was in plain view.
propositions.quote: it was not unreasonable, given the appellants’ very limited privacy interest, for the officer to open the bag. At that point, the cash was in plain view

propositions.text: The officer testified that papers were often dispersed in a bag like the duffle bag and felt paper inside when pressing it.
propositions.quote: the officer’s evidence that relevant papers were frequently dispersed around a cab, often collected in a bag similar to the one at issue here, and that when he “pushed down on the duffel bag, [he] felt and heard paper products inside”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer reasonably opened the duffle bag after feeling paper inside, with cash then in plain view.

propositions.text: The appellants rely on R. v. Jarvis to support the predominant purpose test.
propositions.quote: The appellants’ Reliance on the Jarvis Case Is Misplaced

propositions.text: Jarvis does not support the predominant purpose test here because the context was always penal, unlike Jarvis's civil audit context.
propositions.quote: The present case is wholly different. We are not “crossing the Rubicon” from a civil dispute into penal remedies... The context was always penal

propositions.text: Jarvis requires separation between audit and penal investigative functions; predominant purpose of penal liability triggers Charter protections.
propositions.quote: there must be some measure of separation between the audit and [penal] investigative functions... “predominant purpose of a particular inquiry is the determination of penal liability”

propositions.text: The issue is whether the police search of the duffle bag invaded reasonable privacy interests under the totality of circumstances.
propositions.quote: The issue here is whether the police search of the duffle bag did “in the totality of the circumstances” invade the reasonable privacy interest of the appellants

propositions.text: The court holds the search did not invade the appellants' reasonable privacy interests.
propositions.quote: I would hold that it did not

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the appellants' Jarvis reliance, holding the search did not invade privacy under the totality of circumstances.

propositions.text: The Crown proved on a balance of probabilities that the warrantless search was authorized, reasonable, and met the Collins test.
propositions.quote: the Crown established on a balance of probabilities that the warrantless search was authorized by s. 63(5) of the H&TA... The Collins test is therefore satisfied

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the warrantless search was authorized, reasonable, and satisfied the Collins test.

propositions.text: The trial judge concluded the arrest was invalid.
propositions.quote: The trial judge concluded that the arrest was invalid

propositions.text: Reasonable and probable grounds is a legal standard subject to appellate review.
propositions.quote: The existence of reasonable and probable grounds is a legal standard and is subject to appellate review

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found the arrest invalid; reasonable and probable grounds is a legal standard subject to appellate review.

propositions.text: Discovery of cash alone may not constitute reasonable grounds to arrest, but can contribute when circumstances create reasonable inference of proceeds of crime.
propositions.quote: The discovery of a large sum of cash may not on its own constitute objective, reasonable and probable grounds to arrest... but the existence of the cash may contribute

propositions.text: Trial judge held circumstances or evidence must create reasonable inference that money is proceeds of crime.
propositions.quote: ‘circumstances or evidence’ . . . exist that create a reasonable inference that the money is proceeds of crime” (trial judgment, at para. 35)

propositions.text: Context included three men in an empty, improperly licensed truck at midnight on a highway where truck was not entitled to be.
propositions.quote: three men in an empty, improperly licensed truck making a run across the prairies at midnight on a highway where the truck was not entitled to be

propositions.text: Cargo was missing, documents had discrepancies, and $115,000 in small bills wrapped in bundles typical of drug dealings was found.
propositions.quote: The explanation for where the cargo had gone... did not correspond to the documents... The unexplained $115,000 was in bills of small denominations wrapped in bundles which the police officer believed to be typical of drug dealings

propositions.text: Officer testified money packaging was indicative of proceeds of crime, especially drug trade, based on experience and research.
propositions.quote: the type of bundling that was observed there with the elastic bands and the small denominations is indicative of it being involved in proceeds of crime and in particular of the drug trade in my mind

propositions.text: Officer's experience and training support probative value of his evidence on money packaging.
propositions.quote: the officer’s experience and training supported the probative value of his evidence on this point

propositions.text: Cumulative facts provide objective support for officer's reasonable and probable grounds to arrest.
propositions.quote: The cumulative effect of the factual elements previously described provides objective support for the officer’s subjective belief that he had reasonable and probable grounds to make the arrests

propositions.text: The whole of circumstances is greater than sum of parts in assessing grounds for detention and seizure.
propositions.quote: The whole is greater than the sum of the individual parts viewed individually

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the officer had reasonable grounds to arrest based on cumulative suspicious facts and cash packaging evidence.

propositions.text: Search incidental to arrest must serve valid purposes like safety, evidence protection, or trial evidence discovery.
propositions.quote: A search is properly incidental where the police attempt to “achieve some valid purpose connected to the arrest” including “ensuring the safety... protection of evidence... discovery of evidence”

propositions.text: Searching the vehicle for evidence related to possession of proceeds of crime was incidental and reasonable.
propositions.quote: It was clearly “incidental” to this arrest to search the vehicle in which the cash was found for evidence of the criminal activity to which the money related

propositions.text: Officers reasonably believed searching the trailer would serve the purpose of finding evidence related to the crime.
propositions.quote: The officers’ belief that this purpose would be served by a search of the trailer... was itself reasonable

propositions.text: Important to link location and purpose of search to grounds for arrest.
propositions.quote: The important consideration is the link between the location and purpose of the search and the grounds for the arrest

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the search of the vehicle incidental to arrest was reasonable and linked to the crime evidence.

propositions.text: Two-hour delay between arrest and trailer search is not significant and does not undermine connection between arrest and search.
propositions.quote: The lapse of about two hours between the roadside arrest and the search of the trailer’s secret compartment is not significant and did not... undermine the close causal and spatial connection

propositions.text: Delay of several hours between arrest and vehicle search is not inherently problematic.
propositions.quote: In Caslake, the search of the vehicle did not occur until six hours after the arrest, but the Court concluded that such a delay “is not, in and of itself, problematic

propositions.text: Delay explained by impoundment and legal restrictions on driving truck at night; no prejudice to appellants from delay.
propositions.quote: The lack of quick action by the police may be explained by the fact that the truck was impounded... No particular purpose would have been served by shortening the delay... In neither case would such a delay have worked to the prejudice of the appellants

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the two-hour delay before searching the trailer was reasonable and caused no prejudice.

propositions.text: No separate demonstration of reasonable and probable grounds required for search incidental to arrest.
propositions.quote: In these circumstances, no distinct and separate demonstration of reasonable and probable grounds was required

paragraphs.summary: The court states no separate grounds needed for search incidental to arrest.

propositions.text: Trial judge found no exigent circumstances justified warrantless search after arrest.
propositions.quote: once the arrest was made, there were no exigent circumstances that required the officers to further search the trailer without first obtaining a search warrant

propositions.text: Warrantless search was justified by connection to arrest, not exigent circumstances.
propositions.quote: the basis of the warrantless search was not “exigent circumstances” but connection or relatedness

propositions.text: Seizure of marijuana was Charter compliant as discovered during valid search incidental to valid arrest.
propositions.quote: the seizure of the 392 pounds of marijuana was Charter compliant as it was discovered during a valid search for evidence incidental to a valid arrest

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the warrantless search valid due to its connection to arrest, not exigent circumstances, and seizure was Charter compliant.

propositions.text: Inventory searches do not serve valid criminal justice objectives and require lawful authority to admit evidence.
propositions.quote: an inventory search per se does not serve a ‘valid objective in pursuit of the ends of criminal justice’... the search must be conducted under some lawful authority

propositions.text: Corporal Houston’s inventory search was administrative, not incidental to arrest, thus invalid warrantless search under s. 8.
propositions.quote: Corporal Houston’s work was incidental to RCMP administrative procedures rather than to the arrest... did not meet the requirements of a warrantless search

propositions.text: Evidence from inventory search was obtained in breach of s. 8 Charter rights.
propositions.quote: the fruits of the “inventory” search were thus harvested in breach of s. 8

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the inventory search invalid and its evidence obtained in breach of s. 8.

propositions.text: Grant revised s. 24(2) analysis to balance seriousness of breach, impact on accused, and societal interest in trial on merits.
propositions.quote: this Court revised the approach to s. 24(2) and held that the analysis should be reoriented towards: (i) the seriousness of the Charter -infringing state conduct; (ii) the impact upon the Charter -protected interests of the accused; and (iii) society’s interest in having criminal matters adjudicated on their merits

propositions.text: Evidence from inventory search is a technical breach with minimal impact and should be admitted under s. 24(2).
propositions.quote: The evidence... ought not to be excluded... should be classified as a technical breach with a minimal impact on the Charter -protected interests of the appellants

propositions.text: Had officers continued post-midnight search incident to arrest, evidence would have been discoverable then.
propositions.quote: Had the RCMP officers continued their post-midnight search incident to arrest they would have been within their rights to do so

paragraphs.summary: The court applies Grant and admits inventory search evidence as a minimal-impact technical breach under s. 24(2).

propositions.text: The court would dismiss the appeal.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal. Appeal dismissed

propositions.text: Solicitors for appellants and respondent are named.
propositions.quote: Solicitors for the appellants: Brayford Shapiro Law Office, Saskatoon. Solicitor for the respondent: Public Prosecution Service of Canada, Saskatoon

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and notes the solicitors for both parties.
